Reverse Solitaire

Game StrategyInvariants
Game: start from a Peg Solitaire ending and rebuild the starting pattern by jumping backwards.
How to play: click a peg, then an empty hole two steps away over another empty hole — the middle fills in.
Look for the math

Peg solitaire played backwards feels different, yet Winning Ways shows it is the same game: jumping a peg over a hole is jumping a hole over a hole into a peg.

Reverse jumps

On the English board a reverse move is an orthogonal jump of length two from a peg into an empty hole over another empty hole; the middle hole fills. Each jump adds one peg. The nine puzzles reuse the layouts from the forward Peg Solitaire applet: you begin at a finished position (one centre peg, or the skewed / double openings) and rebuild that layout. The logic test solves Cross in five reverse jumps — the dual of the five-jump forward solution.

Holes as pegs

Leibniz preferred reverse play; Berlekamp, Conway and Guy answer that a reverse jump is ordinary solitaire on the complementary board where empty holes are the “pieces.” Visualising full packages is often easier than visualising empties — that is why the page offers reverse as its own applet.

Same packages, flipped

Any forward solution read backwards is a reverse solution. The invariants that rule out some forward goals rule out the same reverse goals, because the reachable positions are the same set.

Try Cross first — six pegs to rebuild, five reverse jumps.
